---
title: "Running a Sequential Trial: Enrollment, Persistence and the Audit Trail"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

In a sequential trial, subjects enroll one at a time over weeks or months, and each
one is assigned to treatment or control on the day they enroll. The statistics of
such designs are covered elsewhere: [Matching on the Fly](matching-on-the-fly.html)
explains the Kapelner–Krieger designs, and [Planning a Study](planning-a-study.html)
covers power and sample size. This article is about operations. It covers what has
to happen between the first enrollment and the final analysis when the trial is
spread over many R sessions, probably several computers, and possibly several people:

* creating the design before the first subject arrives;
* assigning each arrival and saving the design to disk between enrollments;
* making the allocation reproducible, so that an interrupted trial continues exactly
  as an uninterrupted one would have;
* recording responses that arrive late or out of order;
* what to do when some responses never arrive;
* keeping an audit trail from which anyone can reproduce the allocation;
* the final analysis.

It assumes the four steps of an EDI (Experimental Design and Inference) analysis
(design, assign, record responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html).

## The sequential designs

EDI's sequential designs all share the same interface: a `$new()` call before the
trial, then one `add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign()` call per arrival and
one `add_one_subject_response()` call per outcome. Everything in this article
applies to all of them.

| Class | How each arrival is assigned |
|---|---|
| `DesignSeqOneByOneBernoulli` | An independent coin with probability `prob_T` |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneiBCRD` | Complete randomization run sequentially: exactly `round(n * prob_T)` treated at the end (requires `n`) |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneRandomBlockSize` | Permuted blocks of randomly varying size, optionally within strata |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneSPBR` | Stratified permuted blocks of fixed size |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneEfron` | Efron's biased coin toward the arm that is behind |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneUrn` | Wei's adaptive urn |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneAtkinson` | Atkinson's covariate-adjusted biased coin |
| `DesignSeqOneByOnePocockSimon` | Pocock–Simon minimization over categorical strata |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneKK14` | Matching on the fly with a Mahalanobis distance |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21` | Matching on the fly with weights learned from the responses so far |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21stepwise` | As KK21, with stepwise weights |

The running example uses `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21`, because it is the one design whose
assignments depend on the responses recorded so far, which makes the order of events
part of the allocation. That is the hardest case for persistence and auditing; a trial
run with any other design in the table is a special case of it.

## The trial

Sixty patients enroll over about seven months, with three baseline covariates
recorded at enrollment. The outcome is measured at a follow-up visit eight weeks
later, give or take two weeks, so outcomes come back in a different order from the
one in which patients enrolled, and for most of the trial the most recent patients'
outcomes are still unknown.

In a real trial the arrival dates, covariates and outcomes come from the clinic. Here
they are simulated, all in advance, so that nothing below draws random numbers except
the design itself. `y0` is the outcome each patient would have under control; the
treatment adds `true_effect`.

```{r trial-data}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 60
X = data.frame(age_z = round(rnorm(n), 2), severity = round(rnorm(n), 2),
               biomarker = round(rnorm(n), 2))
true_effect = 0.5
y0 = 1.5 * X$severity + 0.8 * X$biomarker + rnorm(n)

day_enrolled = sort(round(cumsum(rexp(n, rate = 1 / 3.5))))   # one arrival every 3.5 days
day_outcome  = day_enrolled + round(runif(n, 42, 70))          # follow-up 6 to 10 weeks later
start = as.POSIXct("2027-01-04 09:00", tz = "UTC")
```

The trial's history is a list of events, in calendar order. An enrollment is always
before that patient's outcome; on a day with both kinds of event, the enrollment
goes first.

```{r trial-events}
events = rbind(
  data.frame(day = day_enrolled, type = "enroll",  subject = seq_len(n)),
  data.frame(day = day_outcome,  type = "outcome", subject = seq_len(n))
)
events = events[order(events$day, events$type == "outcome", events$subject), ]
events$time = start + events$day * 86400
rownames(events) = NULL
head(events, 8)
```

## Before the first subject: create the design and save it

Everything that defines the allocation rule is fixed at construction: the class, the
response type, the target sample size `n`, the design's tuning arguments, and the
`seed`. Write these into the protocol.

* **Set `n`.** The Kapelner–Krieger designs need it, since their burn-in
  (`t_0_pct * n` subjects) and their matching threshold depend on it, and EDI's
  fixed-sample analysis assumes that the number of subjects was fixed before
  enrollment and not chosen by watching the outcomes. The design does not stop
  enrollment for you, but it refuses subject `n + 1` with an error.
* **Fix the covariate list.** Every arrival must be a one-row data frame with the
  same columns, of the same types, measured before assignment. A value whose type
  differs from its column's (a number that arrives as a character string, say) is
  converted to the column's type; if it cannot be (`"1.7a"` for a numeric column),
  the subject is refused with an error naming the column and the design is left as
  it was, so you can correct the value and add the subject again. A missing
  covariate value is allowed: it is imputed (see the `missingness_method` argument).
* **Set `seed`.** With a seed, the design seeds each assignment from the seed and the
  subject's enrollment number, and puts the session's random number stream back
  afterwards. So the seed fixes the whole allocation (given the covariates and, for
  KK21, the outcomes known at each assignment), whatever else the R session does in
  between, and the seed is saved inside the design object. Without a seed
  (`seed = NULL`), assignments draw from the session's random number stream, and an
  exact restart would need that stream's state (`.Random.seed`) saved and restored
  around every assignment; see [Reproducibility](reproducibility.html).

The trial state lives in one file: the design object and the event log. `saveRDS()` stores the whole R6 object, including the
assignments, the responses, the match structure and KK21's weight history; there is
no special save function. Each save writes a temporary file first and then renames it
over the old one, so a crash during a save cannot leave a half-written trial file.

```{r create-trial}
save_trial = function(state, file) {
  tmp = paste0(file, ".tmp")
  saveRDS(state, tmp)
  invisible(file.rename(tmp, file))    # replaces the old file only once the new one is complete
}

trial_seed = 7041
trial_file = file.path(tempdir(), "trial.rds")

des = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(response_type = "continuous", n = n, seed = trial_seed)
save_trial(list(
  design = des,              # carries the seed
  log    = data.frame(time = start[0], event = character(0), subject = integer(0),
                      value = numeric(0))
), trial_file)
rm(des)
```

In practice the file goes somewhere that is backed up, and the copy made after each
enrollment is worth keeping (a dated file name, or a version-controlled directory),
so that a mistaken entry can be undone by going back one file.

## Each arrival: load, assign, save

Two small functions do all the bookkeeping. `enroll()` loads the trial, assigns the
new patient, appends a line to the log, and writes the file back. `record_outcome()`
does the same for an outcome. Neither touches R's random number generator: the
seeded design draws each assignment from its own seed and leaves the session's
stream as it found it, so other work in the same R session neither affects the trial
nor is affected by it.

```{r enroll-functions}
log_event = function(state, time, event, subject, value) {
  state$log = rbind(state$log, data.frame(time = time, event = event,
                                          subject = subject, value = value))
  state
}

enroll = function(file, x_new, time) {
  state = readRDS(file)
  w = state$design$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(x_new)
  state = log_event(state, time, "assign", state$design$get_t(), w)
  save_trial(state, file)
  w
}

record_outcome = function(file, subject, y, time) {
  state = readRDS(file)
  state$design$add_one_subject_response(subject, y)
  state = log_event(state, time, "outcome", subject, y)
  save_trial(state, file)
  invisible(y)
}
```

Now run the trial, one event at a time. Every call reads the file from disk and
writes it back, as it would if each enrollment happened on a different day in a
different R session. The `runif()` line stands in for whatever else the session does
between enrollments.

```{r run-trial}
w_assigned = rep(NA_integer_, n)
for (e in seq_len(nrow(events))) {
  i = events$subject[e]
  if (events$type[e] == "enroll") {
    w_assigned[i] = enroll(trial_file, X[i, , drop = FALSE], events$time[e])
  } else {
    record_outcome(trial_file, i, y0[i] + true_effect * w_assigned[i], events$time[e])
  }
  invisible(runif(10))    # other work in the session
}
state = readRDS(trial_file)
c(enrolled = state$design$get_t(), treated = sum(state$design$get_w()),
  pairs = max(state$design$get_block_ids()))
```

The subject index `t` that `add_one_subject_response()` takes is the enrollment
order, so the trial's own patient identifiers need a lookup table to `t`; here they
coincide.

## Saving and restoring is exact

Because each assignment is seeded from the trial's seed and the subject's enrollment
number, stopping and restarting the trial makes no difference to the allocation. To
check, rerun the same events in a single session, holding the design in memory and
never saving it:

```{r uninterrupted}
uninterrupted = function(events, seed, skip_outcomes = integer(0)) {
  d = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(response_type = "continuous", n = n, seed = seed)
  for (e in seq_len(nrow(events))) {
    i = events$subject[e]
    if (events$type[e] == "enroll") {
      d$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[i, , drop = FALSE])
    } else if (!(i %in% skip_outcomes)) {
      d$add_one_subject_response(i, y0[i] + true_effect * d$get_w()[i])
    }
  }
  d
}
des_mem = uninterrupted(events, trial_seed)
c(same_assignments = identical(des_mem$get_w(), state$design$get_w()),
  same_pairs = identical(des_mem$get_block_ids(), state$design$get_block_ids()))
```

Both runs give the same 60 assignments and the same pairs.

Nor does the session's other work matter. Here is the same trial with the design kept
in memory and the `runif()` calls sharing R's random number generator between
assignments:

```{r shared-stream}
d_shared = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(response_type = "continuous", n = n, seed = trial_seed)
for (e in seq_len(nrow(events))) {
  i = events$subject[e]
  if (events$type[e] == "enroll") {
    d_shared$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[i, , drop = FALSE])
  } else {
    d_shared$add_one_subject_response(i, y0[i] + true_effect * d_shared$get_w()[i])
  }
  invisible(runif(10))
}
sum(d_shared$get_w() != state$design$get_w())    # assignments that differ
```

None differ. This needs the seed: with `seed = NULL` the design draws from the
session's stream, and the other work in the session would change the assignments
that follow it. That allocation would be just as valid a draw from the design, so the
trial's validity does not depend on the seed. What is lost without one is the ability
to show afterwards that the allocation is the one the seed produces.

The design records the EDI version it was created under. If a design saved under one
major version of EDI is reloaded under another, the first assignment after the reload
gives a warning. Within a trial, keep the EDI version fixed, and record it:

```{r version}
state$design$get_edi_version_created()
```

## Outcomes that arrive late or out of order

`add_one_subject_response(t, y)` records the outcome of the subject enrolled `t`-th,
whenever it arrives; `t` must be a subject who has already enrolled. With `n` set, the
outcomes can come in any order, which they did here:

```{r out-of-order}
outcome_order = state$log$subject[state$log$event == "outcome"]
head(outcome_order, 15)
```

Recording an outcome a second time replaces the first value with a warning
("Overwriting previous response for t = ..."). Use this to correct a data-entry
error, and log the correction like any other event.

**What late outcomes do to KK21.** Every design except KK21 and KK21stepwise ignores
the outcomes while assigning, so for them the outcomes only need to be recorded before
the analysis. KK21 is different: at each assignment it estimates its covariate weights
from the outcomes recorded *at that moment*. Until at least $2(p+2)$ outcomes are
in ($p = 3$ covariates here, so 10), it cannot estimate the weights and uses the KK14
rule instead. Here is how many outcomes were known at each assignment, and the first
assignment at which KK21 used weights:

```{r outcomes-at-assignment}
ev_log = state$log
known_at_assignment = sapply(which(ev_log$event == "assign"),
                             function(k) sum(ev_log$event[seq_len(k)] == "outcome"))
iw = state$design$get_iteration_weights()
first_weighted = which(!vapply(seq_len(n), function(t) t > length(iw) || is.null(iw[[t]]),
                               logical(1)))[1]
c(burn_in_ends_after = floor(0.35 * n), first_weighted_assignment = first_weighted,
  outcomes_known_then = known_at_assignment[first_weighted])
known_at_assignment[c(20, 30, 40, 50, 60)]
```

For comparison, the same 60 patients with each outcome known as soon as the patient is
assigned (as if the outcome were immediate):

```{r immediate-outcomes}
immediate = events[events$type == "enroll", ]
immediate = immediate[rep(seq_len(n), each = 2), ]
immediate$type = rep(c("enroll", "outcome"), n)
des_immediate = uninterrupted(immediate, trial_seed)
iw_imm = des_immediate$get_iteration_weights()
which(!vapply(seq_len(n), function(t) t > length(iw_imm) || is.null(iw_imm[[t]]),
              logical(1)))[1]
```

With immediate outcomes, KK21 weights from the first assignment after the burn-in.
With the follow-up delay it started at subject `r first_weighted`, and every assignment
used fewer outcomes than there were subjects: when the last patient enrolled, only
`r known_at_assignment[n]` of the earlier 59 outcomes were known. The longer the
follow-up relative to the enrollment period, the larger this gap.

Two practical consequences:

* **The order of events is part of the allocation.** For KK21, the same patients,
  outcomes and seed give a different allocation if the outcomes are recorded at
  different times. To reproduce a KK21 allocation, you need the order in which
  enrollments and outcomes were entered, not just the data. The audit log below
  records it.
* **Record outcomes as soon as they are final.** An outcome that sits in a case report
  form for a month is a month during which KK21 matches on less information. Do not
  hold outcomes back and enter them in a batch. If the follow-up is so long that only
  a few outcomes will be known before enrollment ends, KK21 will spend most of the
  trial applying the KK14 rule, and KK14 is the simpler choice.

## The audit trail

The log saved with the trial has one line per event: when it happened, what it was,
which subject, and the assignment or the outcome.

```{r audit-log}
head(state$log, 10)
table(state$log$event)
```

Together with the protocol's design arguments, the seed, the covariate rows exactly
as they were entered, and the EDI and R versions, this log is enough for anyone to
reproduce the allocation. The replay below starts a fresh design with the same seed
and walks through the log, entering each enrollment and each logged outcome in the
recorded order, and checks every assignment against the log as it goes. Nothing in the
replay depends on the trial file.

```{r replay}
replay = function(log, X, seed) {
  d = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(response_type = "continuous", n = nrow(X), seed = seed)
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(log))) {
    i = log$subject[k]
    if (log$event[k] == "assign") {
      w = d$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[i, , drop = FALSE])
      if (w != log$value[k]) stop("assignment of subject ", i, " does not match the log")
    } else {
      d$add_one_subject_response(i, log$value[k])
    }
  }
  d
}
des_replayed = replay(state$log, X, trial_seed)
identical(des_replayed$get_w(), state$design$get_w())
```

The replay reproduces every assignment. Keep the covariate rows in a format that
stores numbers exactly (an `.rds` file, or a CSV written with full precision): a
covariate rounded on export changes the distances the design computed, and with them
possibly the matches. A full account of where EDI draws random numbers, including in
randomization tests and the bootstrap, is in [Reproducibility](reproducibility.html).

## When some outcomes never arrive

Patients withdraw, move away or miss their follow-up visit. EDI's inference classes
need an outcome for every enrolled subject: building one on a design with a missing
outcome stops with an error. To see this, rerun the trial with the outcomes of two
patients never recorded, as if they had been lost to follow-up:

```{r lost-to-follow-up}
lost = c(12, 41)
des_lost = uninterrupted(events, trial_seed, skip_outcomes = lost)
des_lost$check_experiment_completed()
tryCatch(InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik$new(des_lost, verbose = FALSE),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

The same check refuses an analysis when fewer than `n` subjects enrolled. EDI has no
way to shrink `n` after the fact or to analyze a design with missing outcomes, so the
choices are made outside the design object:

* **Time-to-event outcomes.** A patient lost to follow-up is censored at their last
  contact: record `add_one_subject_response(t, y_L = last_contact, y_R = Inf)` on a
  design with `response_type = "survival"`. The survival analyses handle this, under
  the usual assumption that censoring is independent of the event time. See the
  [survival cookbook](cookbook-survival.html).
* **Other outcomes: get the outcome.** Every effort to ascertain the outcome (a phone
  call, a registry, a late visit) is worth more than any analysis fix.
* **A complete-case analysis, as a secondary analysis.** Enter the completers'
  covariates, realized assignments and outcomes into an analysis-only design, as in
  [Analyzing an Experiment You Already Ran](analyzing-an-existing-experiment.html), and use
  an asymptotic, covariate-adjusted analysis:

```{r complete-case}
keep = setdiff(seq_len(n), lost)
w_all = des_lost$get_w()
y_all = des_lost$get_y()
des_cc = DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = length(keep), response_type = "continuous",
                                  verbose = FALSE)
des_cc$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X[keep, ])
des_cc$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w_all[keep])
des_cc$add_all_subject_responses(y_all[keep])
inf_cc = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_cc, verbose = FALSE)
inf_cc$compute_estimate()
inf_cc$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
```

A complete-case analysis is unbiased only if dropping out is unrelated to the outcome
given the covariates and the treatment, which no data can confirm. It also discards
the matched-pair structure: a pair that lost one member is no longer a pair. And the
analysis design is not the design that made the assignments, so its randomization
test and bootstrap would resample from the wrong mechanism; use only its asymptotic
results. Report it as what it is, together with the number lost in each arm. Imputing
the missing outcomes and then entering them as if they were observed is worse: the
analysis would treat imputed values as data and understate its uncertainty.

## The final analysis

When the last subject has enrolled and the last outcome is in, load the trial file
once more, confirm that it is complete, and analyze the design object as usual. The
recommended analysis for a continuous outcome under a KK design is
`InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik`, described in [Matching on the Fly](matching-on-the-fly.html):

```{r final-analysis}
final = readRDS(trial_file)
des_final = final$design
des_final$check_experiment_completed()

inf = InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik$new(des_final, verbose = FALSE)
inf$num_cores = 1L
inf$compute_estimate()
inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

The randomization test redraws assignments from the design's own mechanism. Give the
inference object its own seed so that the p-value can be reproduced; `set_seed()`
does not disturb the session's random number stream.

```{r final-rand}
inf$set_seed(1)
inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 200, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The same steps apply to every other design and outcome type; the cookbooks list the
analyses for each outcome type (for example the
[continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html)), and `InferenceSuite` runs all of the
analyses that apply to a design.

The sequential designs have no interim analysis or stopping rule: the analysis is run
once, after `n` subjects. Looking at the treatment effect partway through and stopping
when it looks good invalidates the fixed-sample p-values and intervals above.

## Checklist

Before the first subject:

1. Fix the design class and its arguments, `n`, the response type, the covariate list
   and the seed in the protocol, and record the EDI and R versions.
2. Create the design with its `seed` and save it to a backed-up file.

For each arrival:

3. Load the trial file, call `add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign()`, log the
   event with its time, and write the file back.

For each outcome:

4. Call `add_one_subject_response()` with the subject's enrollment index as soon as
   the outcome is final, log it, and save.

At the end:

5. Check `check_experiment_completed()`, replay the log to confirm the allocation, and
   run the prespecified analysis once.
